paragraphs: At first men had no kings but the gods, and no government but theocracy. They reasoned like Caligula, and at that time they reasoned rightly. It takes a long time for feeling to change enough that men can make up their minds to take their equals as masters, in the hope of profiting by it.

From the mere fact that God was set over every political society, it followed that there were as many gods as peoples. Two peoples who were strangers to one another, and almost always enemies, could not long acknowledge the same master, just as two armies giving battle could not obey the same leader. So national divisions led to polytheism, and this in turn gave rise to theological and civil intolerance, which, as we shall see later, are by nature the same.

The Greeks had a fancy for rediscovering their own gods among the barbarians. This came from their way of regarding themselves as the natural Sovereigns of those peoples. But nothing is so absurd as the learning that in our day identifies and confuses the gods of different nations. As if Moloch, Saturn and Chronos could be the same god! As if the Phoenician Baal, the Greek Zeus and the Latin Jupiter could be the same! As if there could still be anything in common among imaginary beings with different names!

Someone may ask how, in pagan times, when each State had its own cult and its own gods, there were no wars of religion. I answer that it was precisely because each State, having its own cult as well as its own government, made no distinction between its gods and its laws. Political war was also theological, and the provinces of the gods were, so to speak, fixed by the boundaries of nations. The god of one people had no right over another. The gods of the pagans were not jealous gods; they shared the empire of the world among themselves. Even Moses and the Hebrews sometimes lent themselves to this view by speaking of the God of Israel. It is true that they regarded as powerless the gods of the Canaanites, a proscribed people condemned to destruction, whose place they were to take. But remember how they spoke of the divisions of the neighboring peoples they were forbidden to attack! “Is not the possession of what belongs to your god Chamos lawfully your due?” said Jephthah to the Ammonites. “We have the same title to the lands that our conquering God has made his own.”[1] Here, I think, is a recognition that the rights of Chamos and those of the God of Israel are of the same nature.

But the Jews were subject to the kings of Babylon and later to those of Syria, and they still stubbornly refused to recognize any god but their own. This refusal was regarded as rebellion against their conqueror, and it brought down on them the persecutions we read of in their history, which have no parallel until the coming of Christianity.[2]

Every religion, therefore, was attached solely to the laws of the State that prescribed it, so there was no way of converting a people except by enslaving it, and there could be no missionaries but conquerors. The obligation to change cults was the law to which the vanquished yielded, so one had to be victorious before suggesting such a change. Far from men fighting for the gods, the gods, as in Homer, fought for men. Each man asked his god for victory and repaid him with new altars. Before taking a city, the Romans summoned its gods to leave it. In leaving the Tarentines their outraged gods, they regarded them as subject to their own and compelled to do them homage. They left the vanquished their gods just as they left them their laws. A wreath for the Jupiter of the Capitol was often the only tribute they imposed.

Finally, along with their empire the Romans had spread their cult and their gods, and they had often adopted those of the vanquished themselves, granting both alike the rights of the city. So the peoples of that vast empire gradually found themselves with multitudes of gods and cults, almost the same everywhere. In this way paganism throughout the known world finally came to be one and the same religion.

It was in these circumstances that Jesus came to set up a spiritual kingdom on earth. By separating the theological system from the political, this made the State no longer one, and it brought about the internal divisions that have never ceased to trouble Christian peoples. The idea of a kingdom of the other world was new, and it could never have occurred to pagans. They therefore always looked on the Christians as real rebels, who, while pretending to submit, were only waiting for the chance to make themselves independent and their masters, and to usurp by guile the authority they pretended, in their weakness, to respect. This was the cause of the persecutions.

What the pagans had feared took place. Then everything changed its aspect. The humble Christians changed their language, and soon this so-called kingdom of the other world turned, under a visible leader, into the most violent of earthly despotisms.

However, since there have always been a prince and civil laws, this double power and conflict of jurisdiction have made good government impossible in Christian States, and men have never succeeded in finding out whether they were bound to obey the master or the priest.

Several peoples, however, even in Europe and its neighborhood, have wanted to preserve or restore the old system, without success. The spirit of Christianity has prevailed everywhere. The sacred cult has always remained or again become independent of the Sovereign, and there has been no necessary link between it and the body of the State. Mahomet held very sound views and linked his political system together well. As long as the form of his government continued under the caliphs who succeeded him, that government was indeed one, and so far good. But the Arabs grew prosperous, lettered, civilized, slack and cowardly, and were conquered by barbarians. Then the division between the two powers began again. It is less apparent among the Mahometans than among the Christians, but it exists none the less, especially in the sect of Ali, and there are States, such as Persia, where it is continually making itself felt.

Among us, the Kings of England have made themselves heads of the Church, and the Czars have done the same. But this title has made them less its masters than its ministers. They have gained not so much the right to change it as the power to maintain it; they are not its legislators, but only its princes. Wherever the clergy is a corporate body,[3] it is master and legislator in its own country. So there are two powers, two Sovereigns, in England and in Russia, as well as elsewhere.

Of all Christian writers, the philosopher Hobbes alone saw the evil and how to remedy it. He dared to propose reuniting the two heads of the eagle and restoring political unity throughout, without which no State or government will ever be rightly constituted. But he should have seen that the masterful spirit of Christianity is incompatible with his system, and that the priestly interest would always be stronger than that of the State. What has drawn hatred down on his political theory is not so much what is false and terrible in it as what is just and true.[4]

I believe that if the study of history were developed from this point of view, it would be easy to refute the contrary opinions of Bayle and Warburton. One holds that religion can be of no use to the body politic; the other, on the contrary, maintains that Christianity is its strongest support. We should demonstrate to the former that no State has ever been founded without a religious basis, and to the latter that the law of Christianity at bottom does more harm by weakening the constitution of the State than good by strengthening it. To make myself understood, I have only to make the too vague ideas of religion, as they relate to this subject, a little more exact.
